chapter_summary:
Since 2012, the Raspberry Pi has evolved through many models. Each generation improves performance, connectivity, and power efficiency while keeping the same 40-pin GPIO header so that older accessories and projects remain compatible.

The **Raspberry Pi 5**, released in 2023, is the most powerful model in the standard form factor. It uses a Broadcom BCM2712 quad-core ARM Cortex-A76 CPU running at 2.4 GHz, includes a VideoCore VII GPU, and supports up to 8 GB of LPDDR4X RAM. It has dual 4K HDMI outputs, two USB 3.0 ports, two USB 2.0 ports, Gigabit Ethernet, dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0, and a dedicated power button. It also adds a PCIe connector for high-speed expansion and a fan connector for active cooling. The Pi 5 requires a 5V 5A USB-C power supply for full performance and is best for desktop use, media centers, AI inference, robotics, and demanding IoT gateways.

The **Raspberry Pi 4 Model B** was a major leap forward. It was the first Pi to support 4K video, dual displays, and up to 8 GB of RAM. It uses a Broadcom BCM2711 quad-core Cortex-A72 CPU at 1.5 or 1.8 GHz and is still widely used. The Pi 4 is excellent for general-purpose computing, web servers, and most maker projects. It can be powered by a 5V 3A USB-C supply.

The **Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+** and earlier Pi 3 models use a quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU. They are slower than the Pi 4 but still capable for many IoT, sensor, and automation projects. They use a micro-USB power connector and have a single full-size HDMI port.

The **Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W** is a tiny board about half the size of a standard Pi. It has a quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU, 512 MB of RAM, built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and a single micro-USB port for peripherals. It is ideal for space-constrained or low-cost projects such as motion cameras, environmental loggers, and portable devices. The original **Pi Zero W** is even cheaper and slower but still useful for simple tasks.

When selecting a model, consider these factors:

- **Performance:** Does the project need desktop-class performance, or will a slower Zero suffice?
- **Memory:** Will you run multiple services, a database, or a web server? If so, choose 4 GB or 8 GB.
- **Connectivity:** Do you need wired Ethernet, fast Wi-Fi, or Bluetooth?
- **Power:** Will the project run on battery? A Pi Zero uses far less power than a Pi 5.
- **Size and cost:** The Zero family is smaller and cheaper but has fewer ports.
- **GPIO compatibility:** All modern models share the same 40-pin GPIO header.

Key board components include:

- **SoC:** the main processor containing CPU and GPU.
- **RAM chip:** stores running programs and data.
- **USB and Ethernet controller:** manages USB ports and wired networking.
- **GPIO header:** 40 pins for hardware interfacing.
- **MicroSD card slot:** holds the operating system and user data.
- **HDMI ports:** video output.
- **Camera connector:** connects the Raspberry Pi Camera Module.
- **Display connector:** connects official touch displays.
- **Power input:** USB-C on Pi 4/5, micro-USB on older models.

screens.title: Raspberry Pi Models and Specifications
screens.subtitle: How to match performance, ports, and power to your project needs

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson we will compare the most common Raspberry Pi models and learn how their processors, memory, ports, wireless features, and power needs influence real projects. You'll see why the Pi 5 is the best choice for demanding desktop and media workloads, why the Pi 4 remains a versatile general-purpose board, and when a tiny Zero model is the sensible, low-power pick. We'll also identify the board components you interact with most: the system-on-chip, R A M, USB and Ethernet controllers, the 40-pin GPIO header, camera and display connectors, and power input. Practically, this lets you answer questions like: which Pi fits inside a small battery-powered enclosure, and which model will handle a local database or AI inference task. We'll ground every comparison with concrete examples — a home media server, a portable plant monitor, and a battery wildlife camera — and highlight common misconceptions, such as assuming newer always means better for every project or that all Pis require the same power supply. By the end you'll be able to choose a model based on budget, size, connectivity, and performance needs, and point to the exact components on the board that matter for your design. Which project do you want to optimize for first?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Pick the Raspberry Pi model by balancing performance, size, ports, connectivity, and power; all modern models keep the same 40-pin GPIO so many accessories stay compatible.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this module you will develop four practical competencies. First, you will compare major Raspberry Pi models by reading their specifications and mapping C P U, R A M, and ports to project needs. For example, you'll learn to spot when a Pi 5's PCIe and dual 4K outputs justify its higher power draw for a media server. Second, you will understand how processor type, R A M size, ports, wireless features, and power requirements affect performance and use cases. You will practice deciding whether a device needs desktop-class processing or a low-power controller. Third, you will be able to select the right model for a project by balancing budget, size, connectivity and power constraints; a battery wildlife camera may favor a Zero model while an AI gateway favors Pi 5. Fourth, you will identify key board components, such as the SoC, R A M chip, USB and Ethernet controller, camera and display connectors, and the 40-pin GPIO header. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic that links the skill to a real example, and a verified competency milestone you can use to self-assess readiness.

keyIdea.text: Compare models, understand specs, choose appropriately, and identify board components for confident hardware decisions.

screens.title: Evolution of Raspberry Pi Models
screens.subtitle: How form factors and compatibility evolved since 2012

narration.text: Let's chart how Raspberry Pi models evolved and why that history matters when you pick hardware today. The platform started with earlier single-board designs and matured through Pi 3, Pi 4, and now Pi 5, while the Zero family introduced a minimal, low-power form factor. Important continuity: modern Pis keep the same 40-pin GPIO header, which preserves accessory compatibility across many generations. That matters when you inherit a project or buy HATs and cables. The timeline also shows a steady increase in processing power and connectivity. The Pi 3 family brought built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth widely to the platform, enabling untethered IoT devices. The Pi 4 introduced desktop-class features such as dual 4K support and higher R A M options up to 8 GB, making it a flexible general-purpose board. The Pi 5 further advances C P U architecture and adds PCIe, fan and power-button features, increasing suitability for demanding applications. A common misconception is equating the newest release to the best choice for every project. In practice, a lighter-weight Zero may be the better fit for battery-powered or size-constrained builds. As you review the timeline, ask yourself: does your project need the extra C P U and ports, or will a small, lower-power board meet requirements more simply?

keyIdea.title: Timeline insight
keyIdea.text: Raspberry Pi models improved performance and features over time while preserving GPIO compatibility, letting you reuse many accessories across generations.

screens.title: Raspberry Pi 5 — Features and Use Cases
screens.subtitle: What makes Pi 5 suitable for desktop and demanding projects

narration.text: The Raspberry Pi 5 is the most capable standard-form-factor board in the series and is best when you need desktop-class performance or heavy input and output. Its system-on-chip contains a quad-core ARM Cortex-A76 C P U running at 2.4 gigahertz and a VideoCore VII G P U, and it supports up to eight gigabytes of LPDDR4X R A M. These specifications let you run more simultaneous services, handle media playback at dual 4K resolution, and perform heavier compute workloads such as local inference or robotics control. Pi 5 adds PCIe connectivity for high-speed expansion, a fan connector for active cooling under sustained load, and a dedicated power button for convenient shutdowns. All of that comes at a cost: the Pi 5 needs a 5 volt, 5 amp USB-C power supply for full performance, and it consumes more energy than smaller models. A common misconception is that you always need the Pi 5 for 'faster is better' — but if your project is a tiny battery-powered sensor or a headless logger, the Pi 5 will overdeliver and waste power and space. Consider Pi 5 when your use case demands dual 4K outputs, PCIe devices, or sustained C P U throughput. Could your project justify the higher power and size requirements?

keyIdea.title: Pi 5 summary
keyIdea.text: Use Pi 5 for desktop-class media, AI inference, robotics, and demanding gateways that need PCIe and higher sustained performance; expect higher power requirements.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Pi 5 Features
Core Concept

Raspberry Pi 5

High-performance board with PCIe, fan connector, and dual 4K outputs. Best for media, desktop, AI inference, and robotics.

Processor & RAM
Broadcom BCM2712: quad-core Cortex-A76 at 2.4 GHz. Up to 8 GB LPDDR4X supports multiple services and heavier workloads.
I/O & Expansion
Dual 4K HDMI, USB 3.0 ports, PCIe connector for NVMe or other expansion, Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Power & Cooling
Requires 5V 5A USB-C for full performance. Fan connector supports active cooling under sustained load.
Concrete Example
Home media server with hardware acceleration

Pi 5 can stream dual 4K displays and transcode media while running background services like a local database and a web UI.

Common Mistake
Choosing Pi 5 for every project because it is newest. Often unnecessary for small battery or headless tasks.
Key Takeaway

Use Pi 5 when you need sustained CPU performance, expansion via PCIe, and multiple high-resolution displays; otherwise a lighter model may be preferable.

screens.title: Pi 4 Model B — Versatile General-Purpose Board
screens.subtitle: Why Pi 4 remains a practical choice for many projects

narration.text: The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B marked a major step for the platform by delivering desktop-capable features while remaining energy efficient for many maker projects. Its Broadcom BCM2711 quad-core Cortex-A72 C P U, available at 1.5 or 1.8 gigahertz in certain revisions, supports up to eight gigabytes of R A M. Dual 4K display support, USB-C power, and a mix of USB 3.0 and USB 2.0 ports made the Pi 4 flexible for media playback, light server work, and development tasks. For many learners and makers it strikes a good balance: more capable than Pi 3 family boards for multitasking and higher-bandwidth peripherals, yet less power-hungry and simpler to integrate than a full Pi 5 setup. A common misconception is that Pi 4 cannot run as a headless IoT device; in fact it can be configured for headless operation and is often used for web servers, small databases, and local automation services. When you need a reliable general-purpose board that supports modern peripherals without the highest power requirements, Pi 4 is typically the pragmatic choice. Pi 4 Model B — Versatile General-Purpose Board means pi 4 balances performance and practicality—dual 4k support and up to 8 gb ram make it ideal for general-purpose computing and media tasks without pi 5's peak power needs.. In practical terms, why pi 4 remains a practical choice for many projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pi 4 summary
keyIdea.text: Pi 4 balances performance and practicality—dual 4K support and up to 8 GB RAM make it ideal for general-purpose computing and media tasks without Pi 5's peak power needs.

screens.title: Pi 3 and Earlier Models — When Less Is Enough
screens.subtitle: Understanding the place of earlier models for IoT and automation

narration.text: Older Raspberry Pi models, like the Pi 3 family, continue to be useful for many projects even though they are slower than modern Pis. The Pi 3 models use a quad-core Cortex-A53 C P U and typically include built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, making them suitable for many IoT, sensor, and automation projects. Their single full-size HDMI and micro-USB power connectors reflect earlier hardware decisions and lower power envelopes. The main point is that for projects that do not require desktop performance, a Pi 3 offers a practical balance of connectivity and capability at lower cost. It is common to assume that only Pi 4 or Pi 5 are worth using, but a Pi 3 can be the simplest, most power-efficient choice for headless monitoring, local control loops, or tasks where bandwidth and advanced video output are not required. When considering legacy code or existing hardware, the Pi 3 family often makes migration easier than switching to a radically different form factor. Ask whether your project needs more processing headroom, or whether an older, cheaper board meets your needs efficiently. Pi 3 and Earlier Models — When Less Is Enough means pi 3 boards remain valuable for iot, sensors, and automation where built-in wireless and lower power use fit the task without needing the latest performance.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pi 3 family and predecessors

Match board capability to the problem: older Pis are efficient choices when you don't need advanced video or expansion options.

screens.title: Pi Zero Family — Tiny and Low-Power
screens.subtitle: When to choose a Zero model for size- and power-constrained projects

narration.text: The Pi Zero family provides a very small, low-cost option for projects where space and power are the primary constraints. The Pi Zero 2 W builds on that tiny form factor with a quad-core Cortex-A53 C P U, 512 megabytes of R A M, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. These specifications make the Zero 2 W suitable for motion cameras, environmental loggers, and portable devices where a standard Pi would be too large, too costly, or draw too much power. The original Pi Zero W is even cheaper and a bit slower, but can still handle basic headless tasks. When evaluating a choice, consider physical constraints inside an enclosure, battery life, and whether you need multiple USB ports or full-size HDMI. A common mistake is assuming a tiny board will support many USB peripherals without an additional hub; often a Zero needs adapters or a powered hub for multiple devices. If your project needs very low power draw and small size — for example a wildlife camera inside a waterproof case — the Zero family is the recommended option. Reflect: what are the smallest connectors or external components you must fit inside your enclosure?

keyIdea.title: Zero family summary
keyIdea.text: Choose Pi Zero models when size, cost, and low power draw are the priority; they are ideal for cameras, portable monitors, and small sensor nodes.

Definition

Pi Zero 2 W and Pi Zero W

Ultra-compact boards with modest CPUs and limited ports. Excellent for projects where enclosure size and battery life are decisive.

Zero 2 W specs
Quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU and 512 MB RAM, built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, single micro-USB for peripherals.
Use cases

Battery wildlife camera

Common Mistake

Key Takeaway

screens.title: How to Choose the Right Pi Model
screens.subtitle: A decision checklist that maps requirements to model choices

narration.text: Choosing the right Raspberry Pi is a process of mapping project requirements to model strengths. Start by clarifying performance needs: do you need desktop-class processing for media or AI, or only single-threaded, low-power data collection? Next consider memory: run a database or multiple services and choose 4 or 8 gigabytes; for single-task sensor code, 512 megabytes or 1 gigabyte may be sufficient. Then evaluate connectivity: wired Gigabit Ethernet and USB 3.0 are important for servers and fast peripherals; built-in dual-band Wi-Fi and Bluetooth simplify wireless deployments. Power is critical: if you plan battery operation, prioritize Zero models or Pi 3; for sustained high-performance tasks, plan for a 5 volt 5 amp supply as required by Pi 5. Finally, weigh size and cost against your enclosure and budget constraints. A simple decision flow: if you need PCIe or dual 4K, choose Pi 5; else if you need many ports and more R A M, Pi 4; if small and battery-run, Pi Zero; if moderate wireless IoT work, Pi 3. A common misconception is to prioritize only C P U speed; instead, consider how ports, R A M and power interact to deliver the experience you need. Which branch of the checklist best fits your current project?

keyIdea.title: Decision checklist
keyIdea.text: Map performance, memory, connectivity, power, size, and cost to the model choices: Pi 5 for highest performance, Pi 4 for balance, Pi 3 for basic IoT, and Zero for small/battery projects.

Checklist to choose a model

Follow these steps to translate project constraints into a model selection.

Do you need desktop-class CPU and GPU? If yes, consider Pi 5; if no, smaller models may suffice.
2

3

Require wired Gigabit and many USB 3.0 devices? Lean Pi 4 or Pi 5. Need built-in wireless for remote deployment? Pi 3 or Zero 2 W may suffice.
4

Concrete scenario
Smart mirror

A Pi 4 with higher RAM handles a browser-based dashboard and local services without the Pi 5's higher power needs.

Common Mistake
Focusing only on raw CPU; ports and RAM often determine whether the device can run your full stack.
Key Takeaway

Use a checklist: performance, RAM, connectivity, power, size, cost. Follow the branches to arrive at the suitable model for your project.

screens.title: Key Board Components and Their Roles
screens.subtitle: Identify the SoC, RAM, controllers, connectors and why they matter

narration.text: Understanding the board components helps you plan hardware and software around limits and capabilities. The SoC, or system-on-chip, contains the C P U cores and G P U and determines raw compute and graphics capability. The R A M chip stores running programs and data; more R A M enables more simultaneous services and larger in-memory data processing. The USB and Ethernet controller provides and coordinates USB ports and wired networking; its capabilities determine throughput and the kind of peripherals you can attach. The 40-pin GPIO header provides general-purpose input/output lines for sensors, actuators, and HATs — its pinout and voltage levels are central to hardware interfacing. The microSD card slot holds the operating system and user files; speed and card quality influence boot time and sustained input and output. HDMI ports, camera and display connectors determine whether the board can drive displays or camera modules directly. Power input type — USB-C on Pi 4 and Pi 5 versus micro-USB on older boards — matters for available current and connector robustness. A common mistake is assuming all USB ports are equal; USB 3.0 offers higher bandwidth than USB 2.0. When you design a system, list the components you will use and match them to the board features before buying. Which three components will define your next project?

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: SoC and RAM determine performance, controllers govern I/O and networking, and connectors determine what peripherals or displays you can attach; match these to your project needs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Board Components
Definition

Key components and functions

Know what to look for: the SoC drives computation, RAM holds active data, controllers manage I/O, and connectors link cameras and displays.

SoC
Contains CPU and GPU. Determines the board's processing and graphics capabilities for tasks like media playback and inference.
RAM
Stores running programs and in-memory data. More RAM supports running multiple services or larger data sets.
USB & Ethernet controller
Manages USB ports and wired networking. Bandwidth and protocol versions affect connected peripheral performance.
GPIO header
40-pin header for digital I/O, PWM, I2C, SPI. Central to interfacing sensors and HATs across models.
Practical check
List required connectors

Before buying, list camera, display, USB and Ethernet needs and verify the board provides the correct connectors and controller capabilities.

Misconception
Assuming all USB ports deliver the same speed. Distinguish USB 3.0 from USB 2.0 when bandwidth matters.
Key Takeaway

Identify the three components that will most affect your project—SoC, RAM, and I/O controllers—and match them to your requirements.

screens.title: Create a Model Comparison Table
screens.subtitle: A practical exercise linking specs to project choices

narration.text: Now we'll walk through a hands-on activity: creating a model comparison table of at least three Raspberry Pi models. The goal is to list C P U, R A M, USB ports, networking, power input, and an approximate price for each model and then recommend a model for each sample project. For example, list Pi Zero 2 W with a quad-core Cortex-A53, 512 megabytes R A M, a single micro-USB peripheral port, built-in wireless, micro-USB or USB-C adapter power, and low price; recommend it for a battery wildlife camera. For a smart mirror, list Pi 4 with up to 8 gigabytes R A M, dual HDMI, USB 3.0 ports, Gigabit Ethernet, and a 5 volt 3 amp supply, and justify the choice by display capability and local service needs. For a home media server, give Pi 5 its C P U and PCIe expansion, mention the 5 volt 5 amp supply, and explain how PCIe or USB 3.0 supports fast storage. A common mistake is to compare only C P U cores; include R A M, ports and power in your table. After you build the table, write a short justification for each project choice describing the single most important reason you selected that model.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Build a comparison table and pick models for specific projects, justifying choices by the most important constraint: size, power, ports, or compute.

screens.title: Assessment: Model Recommendation Exercise
screens.subtitle: Apply what you've learned to recommend a model for a constrained project

narration.text: For a short assessment, choose a Raspberry Pi model for a constrained project and justify your recommendation. Consider the wildlife camera example: the board must fit inside a small waterproof case, run on battery for long periods, and upload occasional images over Wi‑Fi. Based on these constraints, the Pi Zero 2 W or Pi Zero W is the expected recommendation because of their small size, integrated wireless, and lower power consumption. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards summarizing the chapter

narration.text: Let's close with three core concepts to carry forward. First, model selection is a trade-off: performance, size, ports, connectivity, and power must be balanced. Keep the project's primary constraint in mind and compare specifications against that constraint. Second, all modern Raspberry Pis maintain the 40-pin GPIO header so many accessories and HATs remain compatible even across generations; that continuity reduces integration effort. Third, power requirements are decisive: Pi 4 and Pi 5 need higher current supplies and, in the case of Pi 5, may need active cooling or a fan connector under sustained load. For battery or sealed-enclosure projects, prioritize the Zero family. These takeaways help you quickly filter models and identify the components that affect your design choices. When you next plan a Pi-based project, ask: which one or two constraints will determine the model choice?

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Balance constraints, prefer GPIO continuity, and always check power needs early in your design.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
Trade-offs matter
Choose by performance, power, ports and size. The single dominant constraint should guide selection.
GPIO continuity
The 40-pin GPIO header is preserved across modern models, enabling reuse of many accessories.
Power first
Verify power input and current requirements early; Pi 5 needs a 5V 5A supply in full-load scenarios.
Summary

Filter models by your project's most important constraints, confirm GPIO compatibility, and check power needs before finalizing hardware choices.

Pi Zero family: small, low-power and affordable, ideal for battery-powered or space-limited deployments such as cameras or portable monitors.
